title: Louisiana Visa Fraud Ringleader Patel Sentenced to 10 Years, Faces Removal
excerpt: Chandrakant Patel recruited foreign nationals and paid four Louisiana law-enforcement leaders to certify fictitious armed robbery reports supporting fraudulent U visa applications, USCIS said.
body:
• Chandrakant "Lala" Patel, 40, of Oakdale, Louisiana, has been sentenced to 120 months — 10 years — in federal prison for conspiracy to commit visa fraud and engaging in monetary transactions in property derived from unlawful activity, USCIS said.
  • Four former law enforcement leaders who helped him — the police chiefs of Glenmora, Oakdale and Forest Hill and the Ward 5 marshal in Oakdale — were each sentenced to 60 months, with three ordered to pay a $30,000 fine.
  • According to court documents, from about November 2020 to July 2025 Patel recruited foreign nationals seeking legal status, took payments, and had them falsely named as victims in fictitious armed robbery reports used to support fraudulent U visa applications.
  • For anyone seeking status in the US: Patel will be removed from the United States after his sentence, and the case is a warning against intermediaries who promise immigration benefits through fabricated documents — a genuine U visa is for victims of qualifying crimes who assist law enforcement.

Chandrakant "Lala" Patel, a 40-year-old businessman from Oakdale, Louisiana, has been sentenced to 10 years in federal prison for running a visa fraud scheme built on armed robberies that never happened, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said. Patel pleaded guilty on May 28 to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and engaging in monetary transactions in property derived from unlawful activity. Upon completion of his sentence, he will be removed from the United States.

How the scheme worked

According to court documents cited by USCIS, the scheme ran from about November 2020 to July 2025. Patel recruited foreign nationals who were seeking legal status in the United States and accepted payments to have them falsely identified as victims in fictitious armed robbery reports. He then paid four public servants to prepare false police reports and certify immigration documents used to support fraudulent U visa applications.

A U visa, USCIS notes, is an immigration benefit available to certain noncitizens who are victims of qualifying crimes and who assist law enforcement in investigating or prosecuting those crimes. The Oakdale scheme manufactured the crime, the victim status and the law-enforcement certification that the benefit requires.

The four officials who certified the false reports

Court evidence showed the four co-conspirators used their law-enforcement positions to certify the false reports, USCIS said. Tebo Onishea, 39, of Glenmora, was chief of police for the City of Glenmora; Chad Doyle, 56, of Oakdale, was chief of police for the City of Oakdale; Michael Slaney, 65, of Oakdale, was marshal of the Ward 5 Marshal's Office in Oakdale; and Glynn Dixon, 63, of Forest Hill, was chief of police for the City of Forest Hill.

Onishea was sentenced on September 2 to 60 months in federal prison, followed by two years of supervised release. Doyle was sentenced on September 15 to 60 months and ordered to pay a $30,000 fine, followed by two years of supervised release. Slaney was sentenced on September 16, 2026, to 60 months and a $30,000 fine, followed by two years of supervised release. Dixon was sentenced on November 9 to 60 months and a $30,000 fine, followed by two years of supervised release. Records also show the conspirators transmitted fraudulent documents through the U.S. mail and other interstate carriers to advance the scheme, USCIS said. Further sentencing details were also reported in coverage of the Oakdale case.

The investigation

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement. The case was investigated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation, and USCIS's Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate, as part of the Homeland Security Task Force under Operation Take Back America, USCIS said. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys John W. Nickel and Danny Siefker.

What this means for applicants

The case does not change the U visa programme itself: genuine victims of qualifying crimes who cooperate with law enforcement remain the people the benefit is for. What it shows is how the certification step can be abused when applicants pay an intermediary and local officials sign false reports. Anyone approached with an offer to be named as a crime victim in exchange for payment is being offered a federal crime, not a shortcut to status. USCIS asks the public to report suspected immigration benefit fraud through its tip form, linked from the agency's announcement above.
